title: Meekness, Not Weakness
author: Catholic Manhood
summary: Writing as Nick of Catholic Manhood, the author argues that meekness has been stolen and recast as timidity, when its original sense is strength under control, like a trained warhorse that holds steady under fire. He contrasts it with weakness, which he defines as ungoverned strength: a man whose anger fires at inconvenience while he stays silent at injustice, whose word and love last only while they are cheap. He finds the pattern in Aragorn, who could have taken the Ring and instead served unrecognised for years, and above all in Christ in Gethsemane, whose silence was power perfectly ordered rather than passivity. The practical section describes how a meek man conducts himself: he listens before he speaks, does not need to win every argument, leads by being worth following, endures without performing his suffering, is gentle with those in his care and fierce when justice requires. The piece is devotional in register but its subject is the formation of masculine character, which is why it belongs with the archive's writing on manhood.
points: The central redefinition is that meekness is power under governance, strength in service of something greater than oneself, not passivity or conflict avoidance.
Weakness is defined as the absence of interior order, so a man who cannot govern his urges is weak however strong or loud he is.
Aragorn and Christ in the garden illustrate strength that is real but directed beyond the self, with restraint chosen rather than imposed.
The practical profile includes listening before speaking, conceding when wrong, leading by being followed willingly, and enduring without performance.
The author insists meekness is not safe, since the meek man is fierce when justice is violated and angry only in an ordered way.
quotes: Meekness is a word that has been taken from us and warped into something it was never meant to mean. Our world has decided that meek means timid or passive.
Obviously, the warhorse was not weak. In fact, it was one of the most powerful creatures in existence. Through discipline, it rejected weakness and gained precision.
Meekness is power under governance. Meekness is strength in service of something greater that self.
A man who cannot govern his urges and appetites is weak no matter how much he can lift or how loudly he speaks.
Aragorn did not lack power. He did all of those things humbly because he knew that the mission at hand was not about him.
A meek man does not feel the need to “win” every argument and learns the difference between being right and being seen to be right. When a meek man is wrong, he says so.

A loud man who needs constant acknowledgement of his authority doesn’t have any. Authority is given and it is given to men who demonstrate that their strength and fire is directed beyond their own advancement.
A meek man endures. A man who suffers loudly for others to notice confuses endurance with performance.
